title: Chandaka sent back
hook: the charioteer begs to stay; the prince sends him home with his jewels (Buddhacarita 6)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the flight, and your line: the gates open. Did you say out loud what you need? Today the night ride ends at the edge of a forest. Day seven hundred seven.

Sunrise, and a horse that has run all night stands blowing at the edge of a hermitage. A young man climbs down. For the first time in his life, there is no palace behind him. Beside him stands Chandaka, the attendant who saddled the horse in the dark and rode out with him. He has done everything he was told all night. Now the prince gives him one more order: go home. And Chandaka says no.
screen: `SUNRISE AT THE HERMITAGE.` → `ONE MORE ORDER: GO HOME.` → `CHANDAKA SAYS NO.`

segments.voice: First, the thanks. Before any parting, the prince praises Chandaka. In the poem he says, in paraphrase, that this loyalty is rare: a man who follows his master when there is nothing to gain by it. The thank-you comes first. Second, the jewels. The prince takes off his ornaments and puts them in Chandaka's hands, with a message for the king. Tell my father, he says, that I haven't gone into the forest out of anger, or for lack of love, or out of longing for heaven. I've gone to put an end to old age and death. Don't grieve for me. Third, the begging. Chandaka weeps. How can I lead this horse home with an empty saddle? What do I say to your father, to the queen who raised you, to your wife? Don't send me back. The prince answers gently, with an image from the poem: beings meet the way birds gather in one tree for the night, and in the morning they fly off in different directions. Parting comes for everyone, he says; this one, at least, has a purpose. Fourth, the last things. With his own sword the prince cuts off his long hair. A hunter in a dull-colored robe passes by, and the prince trades his fine silk clothes for that plain cloth. The poem says the hunter was a god in disguise. Then Chandaka turns for home, slowly, leading Kanthaka, and the poem says the horse licked the prince's feet and wept before he went. Since the old man on the cleared road, the poem has been taking things from the prince one at a time: his ease, a garden's charm, a friend's good argument, the palace. Today it's the jewels, his hair, his clothes and his last companion, and each one goes back with care.
screen: `FIRST, THE THANK-YOU.` · `THE JEWELS AND A MESSAGE.` · `BIRDS IN ONE TREE FOR A NIGHT.` · `HAIR CUT, SILK TRADED.` · then, large: `SENT HOME WITH THE JEWELS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give back one thing you don't need. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you're holding that isn't really yours to keep. A borrowed book. A coat that hasn't left the closet in years. A job on a committee you agreed to long ago. Pick one. Now picture giving it back the way the prince did: thanks first, then a clear word about why, then open hands. No slammed door. When you've pictured it, let your hands rest open in your lap for the rest of the sit. Later today, if it's a thing, give it back for real. The bell holds the time.
Chandaka. The prince's attendant, thanked and sent home from the forest's edge with the horse, the jewels, and a message for the king. Today's word.
Your line: sent home with the jewels. Today, when you let something or someone go, send it off with thanks and one honest sentence about why. Day seven hundred seven.

howItsDone: The cutting of the hair and the change into a plain robe are remembered in Buddhist ordinations, where in some communities a new monk or nun has the head shaved and puts on the robe before taking vows.

fork.setup: you're Chandaka. you've ridden all night beside the prince, and at sunrise he puts his jewels in your hands and tells you to go home. what do you do?
options: weep and beg to stay with him.
pretend to leave, then follow him.
fork.reveal: he weeps and pleads: how can he bring the horse home with an empty saddle? the prince answers that beings meet like birds in one tree for a night, then part, and sends him home.

original.note: Sanskrit: the name of the prince's attendant; Pali tellings call him Channa.

trapdoor: what you thought: the prince just left his servant at the edge of the woods.
what it means: he thanks Chandaka, gives him the jewels and a message, and answers his tears before sending him home.
what a scholar hears: Ashvaghosha gives the servant a full speech of protest, so even this parting is argued out, like the leaving before it.

sources.ref: Buddhacarita 6 (Chandaka dismissed: the thanks, the jewels and message, the pleading, the hair and the robe)

notes: All Buddhacarita material paraphrased (Cowell 1894 is not on the validator list).

Confirm in Cowell canto 6: the praise of Chandaka's loyalty; the message to the king (not from thirst for heaven, lack of love or anger, but to destroy old age and death); Chandaka naming the king, the queen who raised him (Gautami) and Yashodhara; the image of birds gathering in one tree and parting.
Confirm the hunter in a dull-red/ochre robe as a god in disguise, and Kanthaka licking the prince's feet and shedding tears in this canto rather than in canto 8.
The outline calls Chandaka 'the charioteer'; script keeps 'attendant' to match day 706's auditor note. Index wording unchanged.
Week-end look back (days 701-707) is in the last lines of the teach.

Auditor: hook's 'for the first time, Chandaka says no' cut to 'Chandaka says no' (unsourced count claim); the teach's 'better it come now, for a reason, than later, for none' softened to a paraphrase that parting is certain and this one has a purpose; confirm against Cowell canto 6.
